article:
There is a strange gap at the center of musculoskeletal medicine. Anyone with a foam roller and twenty minutes can find [dozens of small, discrete, exquisitely tender points in their own body]{claim=VASO-C001} — most densely around the hips and shoulders, by common report more numerous with each passing decade. Roll across one and it announces itself. Yet open the research literature and you find scientists arguing about what these points are — and, in part, [about whether the “trigger point” is a real, reliably identifiable thing at all]{claim=VASO-C030}.

This case examines a chain of ideas offered to close that gap, and the accounts that compete with it. The chain runs from textbook smooth-muscle physiology, through a minority hypothesis about blood and computation, to Tibetan and Indian contemplative anatomy, and it arrives at a proposal with a slogan: a knot is a *state*, not a *scar* — something the body is actively doing and could stop doing, rather than tissue that has been damaged. The lower rungs of the chain are established science. The upper rungs have never been tested. Three different pictures of what the state might be are now on the table — a latched arteriole inside the muscle, a clenched vessel-and-nerve bundle where it pierces the fascia under the skin, and ordinary neuromuscular guarding dressed in expectation — and the single experiment that would begin to decide among them has never been run.

## A phenomenon without a mechanism

Part of the reason the fight has run so long is structural. Medicine is organized by organ system: orthopedics owns bones, neurology owns nerves, cardiology owns the pipes. Nobody owns muscle tone — the continuous, neurally set background contraction of soft tissue. No specialty means no billing codes, no imaging protocols, no funding lines. The skeptics’ favorite line, “there is no evidence,” is partly circular: there is little evidence in part because nobody has been paid to look.

But the skeptical case deserves its full weight, and it is heavier than proponents usually grant. A systematic review of examination-reliability studies (Lucas and colleagues, 2009) concluded that manual examination for trigger points has not been shown to be reliable or valid — partly because no accepted reference standard exists for what one is — and could not be recommended as an objective diagnostic test. The most pointed peer-reviewed critique (Quintner, Bove and Cohen, 2015) argues that the construct rests on circular reasoning: the lesion has never been demonstrated, examiners disagree, and the clinical phenomena can be explained otherwise. That critique drew a rebuttal, and the exchange rather than either paper is the state of the debate. Even the construct’s defenders concede the core of the complaint: the NIH-affiliated imaging group whose work appears below writes that examination results “can vary depending on the clinician’s training and experience,” and that palpation and pain scores remain the reference standard while being “still subjective measures.” The dispute, then, is not only about mechanism. It reaches the observation base: the reproducibility and even the ontological status of the discrete palpable spot are part of the academic argument. That is why this case grades the first claim above as *provisionally* rather than *well* supported — the shared experience is vast, but the instrumented record behind “discrete” and “palpable” is thinner than it feels under the fingertip. The only population figure the ledger holds is a 1986 clinic-based estimate, quoted second-hand in a 2011 introduction, that myofascial pain affects some 23 million Americans; that is a prevalence for a pain syndrome, not a count of tender points in ordinary people. The essay this case grew from points to fibromyalgia-era community exams using an eighteen-site tender-point protocol, said to find tender points nearly universal with counts tracking distress rather than tissue damage, but the underlying surveys have not been traced in this project, and until they are, the figures carry no weight here.

What survives the critique is a set of instrumented findings, and they deserve to be seen in detail, because they cut both ways. Shah and colleagues (2008) sampled the fluid at active trigger points and found [it more acidic and loaded with mediators of pain and inflammation — bradykinin, substance P, CGRP]{claim=VASO-C005}. The study had about nine volunteers and, as its own title says, the mediators were elevated at sites remote from the points as well as near them. Something is there, and it is chemically angry — but whether what is there is *local* is less settled than it sounds.

The most detailed instrumented look comes from the same NIH lineage. In 2011 Ballyns, Shah and colleagues imaged the upper trapezius of forty-four patients with acute neck pain, 169 sites in all, with the sonographers blinded to which sites the examiner had called active (painful on its own), latent (painful only when pressed), or normal. Vibration sonoelastography — shaking the tissue with a handheld massager and mapping where it fails to move — found [a graded region of stiffness: about 0.57 square centimeters at active points, 0.36 at latent points, and 0.17 at palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C033}, and the area separated the three classes well, with an area under the curve of 0.9 for active against normal. Color Doppler found prominent vessels near the points, and [arteries within a centimeter or two of active points showed a pulsatility index — a measure of how sharply flow surges and falls with each heartbeat — of 8.3, against 3.0 near normal sites]{claim=VASO-C031}, with flow running backward between heartbeats at 55 percent of active sites. That is the finding proponents read as the footprint of something clenched upstream.

The same paper contains the qualifiers. [Backward diastolic flow also appeared near 31 percent of palpably normal sites]{claim=VASO-C032}, so the waveform is a gradient across symptomatic muscle rather than a marker of a knot. [The resistivity index — a companion measure of downstream resistance — did not differ at all between active, latent and normal sites]{claim=VASO-C036}, and the pulsatility index varied so widely that it could not classify any individual site; the authors report that the blood-flow measures “did not perform well as classifiers.” There was no pain-free control group: the “normal” sites were simply five centimeters away in a muscle that had a trigger point somewhere else, and the authors say plainly that their flow findings “do not represent the normal variation.” The vessels interrogated were pulsatile arteries or enlarged arterioles typically more than a millimeter across, one to two centimeters from the point — not the microvessels a latch account would need. And the authors list, as candidate causes of the high-resistance flow, muscle contracture compressing the capillary bed, the anatomy of the trapezius apex, inflammatory vasoconstriction, and pressure from the transducer itself; they never mention smooth-muscle latch. A 2021 systematic review of 33 imaging studies, characterized in this ledger only second-hand, reports that stiffness and blood-flow measures can distinguish active and latent points from healthy tissue, with reproducibility caveats attached. The sum: palpated knots are objectively stiffer, in a graded way, inside the muscle itself, and the local arteries behave somewhat differently — but the vascular signature is partial, and nothing in it says what the stiff tissue is.

Then there is the phenomenology practitioners report, which any candidate mechanism must explain. The obstruction feels like a dull blockage rather than a sharp stretch-pain. Knots accumulate and hold flexibility hostage. And — the strange one — [pressure locates a knot, but release comes with breath: press in, exhale slowly, and something lets go within seconds]{claim=VASO-C004}. Practitioners add that [pressure alone, without the breath, does not seem to release the point]{claim=VASO-C039} — the “two-key” protocol — that fresh knots yield in a session and old ones take months, and that releasing an old, heavily loaded cluster can bring a wave of warmth and euphoria; this case catalogues those reports as untested claims, because no one has rated such an event at the time it happened. As for the release itself, this case labels the report for what it is: first-person testimony from the hypothesis’s own proponent, in an essay whose text was generated by AI models at the author’s direction; consistent with widespread practitioner lore; contradicted by no one; measured by no one. It is real evidence that people *feel* a release. It is no evidence at all that anything happens in the tissue. It is the anchor phenomenon of everything that follows — and the two-key half of it is the part most exposed, because a 2025 elastography study of calf trigger points in runners, located but not yet opened in this project, is reported to show most palpated points undetectable within minutes of pressure alone, with no breath instruction, and absent a day later. If it says what it is reported to say, pressure sufficed. Nothing from it carries weight until it is read.

## Two experiments that catch the loop in motion

The evidence that these spots are under ongoing neural control has existed for decades, largely unread. In 1993, Hubbard and Berkoff inserted fine needle electrodes into trapezius trigger points and, simultaneously, into adjacent non-tender fibers. They recorded sustained spontaneous electrical activity in a one-to-two-millimeter nidus of every trigger point, and none in the non-tender sites, with higher amplitude in tension-headache and fibromyalgia patients than in healthy subjects. The knot is not merely stiffer than its surroundings; it is a small island of maintained activity in muscle nominally at rest. The authors guessed that sympathetically driven muscle-spindle contractions were the source; later literature favors endplate potentials; the generator remains contested.

“None in the non-tender sites” needs a qualifier. Skeletal muscle fibers receive their nerve supply in a band called the motor endplate zone, and faint electrical activity there — endplate noise — is a known finding. In 2002 Simons, Hong and Simons located the endplate zone electrically in eleven muscles of ten subjects and needled three kinds of site. Endplate noise appeared at all eleven trigger-point sites; [it also appeared at four of eleven non-tender sites that lay in the endplate zone but outside any trigger point]{claim=VASO-C034}; and [it never appeared at taut-band sites outside the endplate zone]{claim=VASO-C035}. The authors’ own summary is that the signature is “characteristic of, but is not restricted to,” the trigger point. Put the two studies together and the honest statement of the electrical finding is that [trigger points carry a sustained electrical signature more often than non-tender sites in the same endplate zone, and never where there is no endplate zone at all]{claim=VASO-C002} — a prevalence gradient, eleven of eleven against four of eleven against none, rather than an exclusive island. Hubbard and Berkoff’s silent control sites may simply have lain off the endplate zone. The Simons study was small, nonrandomized and unblinded, and its authors are the construct’s leading proponents; the finding nonetheless cuts against exclusivity, and it says something about where the signature lives: in the endplate zone first, and at the trigger point second.

The follow-up to Hubbard and Berkoff, from McNulty, Gevirtz, Hubbard and Berkoff in 1994, is the remarkable one. With electrodes in place in fourteen subjects, they administered mental arithmetic. [Activity at the trigger point rose; control sites in the same muscle stayed comparatively quiet; the subjects were not tensing]{claim=VASO-C003}. A purely mental event, involving no movement, turned up the signal inside one tender point and not a centimeter away. The brain has the knot’s address. Both studies are small, old, from one lineage, and never replicated with modern instrumentation; neither took any vascular measurement; and — the Simons result again — neither placed its control needle in a matched endplate-zone site, so whether the stressor selected the trigger point or simply any endplate zone is open. The founding essay adds two follow-ups from the same lineage — relaxation training lowering the activity, and an infusion of the alpha-blocker phentolamine quieting the site — and candidate papers for both have been located but not retrieved; until one is, the autonomic-maintenance argument rests on stress induction alone. Note, too, that three different readings of this one result are now live: stress-sensitive endplates (guarding), a sympathetic write to an arteriole inside the muscle (the latch account), and [a regional sympathetic vasoconstriction written to a skin territory, as in blushing or blanching]{claim=VASO-C143} (the perforator account, below). The needle cannot tell them apart. A skin-perfusion camera over the point during the arithmetic could.

Then, in August 2026, a study in *Nature Human Behaviour* supplied the regulatory counterpart. Mizrachi, Rottem and Rozenkrantz induced identical histamine skin-prick inflammation in the same fifty-seven volunteers on different occasions, in preregistered experiments, manipulating only where attention went. [Attending to the inflamed site produced roughly 1.5-fold smaller and faster-resolving wheal-and-flare responses in about ninety percent of participants across two cohorts — with no difference in skin conductance, heart rate, skin temperature or self-reported anxiety, and heart-rate variability higher under inward attention]{claim=VASO-C006}. A local anesthetic dissected two routes: a sensory one that lidocaine degraded and a top-down vagal one that survived it. What this shows is that cognition can write to a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal. What it does not show is anything about knots, smooth muscle, or seconds: the timescale was tens of minutes and the route is vagal immune regulation, in a tissue the authors note the parasympathetic system does not directly innervate. It is an existence proof for a channel, not for any of the featured mechanisms.

## The ratchet in the vessel walls

{plate:IMG-VASO-P02}

The body contains a second muscular system under no direct voluntary command: smooth muscle, lining the blood vessels, gut and airways, answering to autonomic state. Smooth muscle has a property skeletal muscle lacks, textbook physiology since Hai and Murphy formalized it in 1988: [the latch-bridge state, in which its molecular motors grip and then lock, holding tension at a small fraction of the usual energetic cost after the activating signal has faded]{claim=VASO-C010}. In the model, cross-bridges that have been switched off chemically — dephosphorylated — remain attached and detach only slowly, so a vessel can sustain high stress at low levels of activation. Low, not zero: the popular version, in which the signal “disappears entirely and the grip remains,” overstates what the model claims. Arteries must hold tone for a lifetime; the latch is how they afford it. It is a kinetic trap, not damage — latched tissue looks normal under a microscope. And it is history-dependent: the tissue’s present state depends on what was done to it. A cheap, history-dependent hold that persists after its input fades is, in engineering terms, a memory element. Two questions follow. Is anything ever written to it? And does it exist in the vessels a knot would need?

Here the speed of the felt release becomes the crucial clue. Structural change in tissue — remodeling, scarring — takes days to weeks. [A change that completes in seconds, mid-exhale, must be a change of maintained state, not of structure]{claim=VASO-C011}: something the body is doing and can stop doing. Scar tissue does not release on an exhale. The inference is sound, and this case grades it as provisionally supported on physiological priors rather than on any record in its ledger — with two caveats. Its premise, that the felt release corresponds to an objective local event, is precisely the thing never measured. The one imaged change in a trigger point the ledger holds is from the Ballyns study: three active points followed after dry needling shrank on sonoelastography and their pulsatility index fell over subsequent visits — which shows the measures can move, over days, after a needle, and nothing about seconds or breath. And “state” is a bigger tent than “vascular”: sustained motor guarding is a state; so is fascial densification — the proposal, from fascia researchers, that [viscous hyaluronan between fascial layers thickens and then thins again under pressure, movement and warmth]{claim=VASO-C077}. If densification can reverse in seconds, the knot could be a state without being a vessel. Nobody in this ledger has yet retrieved the timescale, which is why the research agenda asks for it.

## What the arteriole record actually says

This is where the case’s own study lands, and it lands against the comfortable assumption. A frozen-criteria evidence map (study VASO-S001) asked a narrow question: where, by vessel type and caliber, has the latch actually been demonstrated with a contemporaneous readout of activation or energetic cost? Sixteen eligible rows, 1981 to 2022, answered three ways.

First, the energetic argument — that a knot could be held for almost nothing — rests entirely on large conduit arteries. Every measurement of oxygen consumption, lactate release or ATP turnover during maintained force comes from swine or porcine carotid preparations held at zero transmural pressure. No arteriole or resistance microvessel of any bed has ever had its holding cost measured. Searches aimed specifically at arteriole energetics returned nothing.

Second, the compartment the original hypothesis names has been examined, and what was found does not look like a latch. Three rows are pressurized rat skeletal-muscle arterioles — cremaster and gracilis, roughly a hundred micrometers across — in which myosin light-chain phosphorylation, the molecular marker of activation, was measured against diameter. In all three, maintained constriction came with maintained or *rising* phosphorylation: 27.7 percent at 30 mmHg rising to 39.6 percent at 120 mmHg in one study; about 40 percent at 10 mmHg rising to about 55 percent at 80 mmHg in another, attributed there to calcium sensitization and actin polymerization. A 2000 paper states flatly that arteriolar tone “represents a state of maintained smooth muscle activation that requires increases in [Ca2+]i and myosin light-chain phosphorylation.” That is the opposite signature to the economical, dephosphorylated hold a latch requires. The cautions are real: none of the three was designed as a latch test; all held their stimulus present throughout, and myogenic tone is by construction a response to a maintained stimulus, so they could not have seen input-free persistence even if it exists; and the rows were built from abstracts. But the assumption that the arteriole was simply unexamined is gone.

Third, latch behavior is not generic across vascular smooth muscle. The one published comparison between a vessel and its own downstream branch — rabbit femoral artery against its saphenous branch — found sustained stress at falling calcium in the parent (42 percent phosphorylation) and a forty-percent stress loss in the branch (28 percent), attributed to motor-protein isoforms that do not support latch-bridge formation. One laboratory, one pair of papers, and nobody has followed the comparison further downstream. Vessel type and motor-protein phenotype are load-bearing variables, not incidental ones.

So the mechanism the knot hypothesis borrows is real where it has been studied, and unobserved — arguably pointed away from — where the original hypothesis needs it. That is not a refutation. It is a mismatch, and a specific gap the research agenda targets. It is also, as the sections below show, the reason a second vascular account has appeared that does not need the latch at all.

## What if blood talks back?

In 2008 the neuroscientists Christopher Moore and Rosa Cao proposed the hemo-neural hypothesis: that coupling between neurons and blood runs both ways — that [local vascular and hemodynamic state can modulate what nearby neurons do]{claim=VASO-C012}, through mechanical, thermal and chemical channels. It was a hypothesis paper; it demonstrated nothing new. Sixteen years later, in 2024, Jammal Salameh and colleagues reported in *Science* that physiological blood-pressure pulsations modulate central neuronal activity through mechanosensitive ion channels, in rat preparations and awake animals, on rapid timescales. The read path has a demonstrated mechanism. It is a mechanism of *instantaneous* modulation, in rat brain: it shows vessels can nudge neurons now, not that vessels can store anything and read it back later. Proponents argue that nothing in the logic is brain-specific and that peripheral sensory endings sit alongside the very vessels whose caliber they would sense. That extension is argument, not yet measurement.

## The synthesis, and what it would explain

The researcher Michael Edward Johnson has assembled these pieces into a program he calls vasocomputation, stated in three hypotheses of ascending ambition: that rhythmic vessel contraction acts as a compression sweep collapsing ambiguous neural patterns; that a vascular contraction freezes local neural patterns for its duration, functioning as a prediction and a medium-term memory; and that a contraction held long enough engages the latch and durably freezes nearby circuitry until the prediction resolves. Write, store, read: [vascular tension as a memory medium participating in mental life — with the grasping Buddhism calls tanha as its felt signature]{claim=VASO-C021}. The program is self-published, not peer-reviewed, and as of 2026 its experiments seek evidence rather than report it. The critical report commissioned for this case adds the sharpest objection: biological memory requires a state that depends on prior input, can later be read out, and discriminates between different prior inputs. A thermostat has hysteresis; it does not have an autobiography. The latch literature addresses none of these criteria, and the report notes that the nearest genuine write–store–read loop in a living flow network is a slime mold storing nutrient locations in the diameters of its own tubes — an organism very unlike us.

Whatever the fate of that grand identification, consider what the stack offers the humble knot. [A knot becomes a latched arteriole throttling its own neighborhood — chronic local ischemia at near-zero energetic cost, producing the acidic, sensitized milieu the microdialysis found, wrapped in secondary skeletal-muscle guarding]{claim=VASO-C020}. This would patch the oldest hole in trigger-point theory: the classic “energy crisis” model needed muscle fibers in permanent maximal contraction, a metabolic bonfire no one could account for, where a latch holds for almost nothing. It would explain why knots feel like autonomous objects, why they persist for years, why the Doppler findings show flow behaving as if something upstream were clenched — remembering that the authors of the Doppler study list muscle contracture compressing the bed as one candidate cause. And it would explain the two-key protocol. Smooth muscle takes no voluntary commands, but it answers to autonomic state, and [slow breathing with extended exhalation reproducibly shifts autonomic balance toward the parasympathetic]{claim=VASO-C013} — a 2018 systematic review documents the rise in heart-rate variability and respiratory sinus arrhythmia across studies of healthy people. Pressure perturbs the local loop; breath shifts the chemistry that governs unlatching. The roller is the read head; the exhale is the write head. Note, though, what the breathing evidence establishes: a global shift, measured on the heart, in people with no tender point in the study. The local, site-specific unlatching the hypothesis adds on top has never been measured.

## Three accounts of a knot, side by side

Strip the case to its live mechanisms and there are three — two vascular, one not — and they make different predictions. A reader should know all three.

### The latched arteriole

*What it proposes.* The account above: a microvessel inside the muscle, held shut by smooth-muscle latch, starving a small territory; the electrical nidus, the acid, and the guarding are downstream. *What it predicts.* A stiff, electrically active spot that is metabolically *cold* on FDG-PET, because a latch burns almost nothing — a triple signature no conventional lesion carries; a latch-competent motor-protein phenotype in skeletal-muscle arterioles; and, at a release, blood returning before stiffness falls. *What the ledger holds.* The latch is real in conduit arteries; the arteriole record shows maintained activation, not a latch; no arteriole’s holding cost has ever been measured; the vessels with abnormal Doppler are conduit-scale, a centimeter or two away; and the critical report finds no study identifying smooth-muscle latch at any tender point. *What would decide it.* A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after its stimulus is withdrawn, at falling phosphorylation; a cold knot on PET; or, against it, a hot one, and the non-latching phenotype all the way down.

### The stuck perforator

*What it proposes.* A second account, set out in the proponent’s companion essay of September 2026, accepts the arteriole audit and moves the vascular element up and out — from arterioles inside the muscle to the small artery-nerve-lymphatic bundles that pierce the superficial fascia on their way to the skin, which surgeons call perforators and locate with a pencil Doppler. A knot, on this picture, is a perforator held in a stuck state, and [what holds it is not one memory element but three, nested: the vessel’s tone, a collar of gelled hyaluronan around the bundle, and the tether the collar makes between the fascial sheet and the tissue beneath]{claim=VASO-C174}, [each staying where it was put after the input that put it there has gone]{claim=VASO-C175}. The skin’s arterioles are among the most sympathetically dominated vessels in the body, so [the bed needs no economical latch to hold a knot; ordinary tonic firing suffices]{claim=VASO-C153}. That drops the latch as a load-bearing part and drops the cold-spot prediction with it. *What it predicts.* That palpated tender points coincide with Doppler-mapped perforators above chance. That [the “star” or spark felt at a release is reperfusion tingling in the skin patch one perforator supplies]{claim=VASO-C099}. That the breath works through a textbook reflex — [a deep inspiration constricts skin arterioles within about two seconds]{claim=VASO-C097}, a slow exhale lets them open — so that [pressure applied during an inhale-and-hold should fail to release a knot]{claim=VASO-C130}. That freeing the collar with a few milliliters of saline under ultrasound should release a knot with no breath at all. That the McNulty result is a regional sympathetic write to a skin territory. And, like the latch account, [blood first, stiffness second]{claim=VASO-C073} — now at the skin surface, where a laser speckle camera can film it. *What the ledger holds.* Nothing, in either direction. Its only source is the proponent’s second essay, whose text was AI-generated and which this ledger has not been able to verify; the published studies it invokes — a 1988 dissection said to place about eighty percent of classical acupoints at fascial perforations, entrapment syndromes described as tender points at fascial rings, conducted vasodilation running upstream along arteriole walls — are catalogued here as its propositions, not as retrieved records. Its parent proposition, that knots simply *are* stuck perforators, is stated as a hypothesis by its author and has no evidence record. It also owes an explanation of the one instrumented fact that fits the intramuscular picture best: the graded stiff regions and hypoechoic nodules the sonographers measured lie inside the trapezius muscle, not in the fascia under the skin. *What would decide it.* An afternoon with a pencil Doppler and two blinded operators — do the tender points sit on the perforators above chance? Then a hydrodissection trial and the inhale-hold block. A null on the coincidence map returns the vascular idea to the muscle, or dissolves it.

### Guarding, densification, and interpretation

*What it proposes.* Tender points are neuromuscular guarding: sustained low-level motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, centrally maintained and stress-sensitive, possibly with altered fascial gliding from hyaluronan densification. Nothing is stored in a vessel. The brain stops guarding, regionally or globally, and interpretation supplies the rest. *What it predicts.* That the electrical signature tracks the endplate zone rather than the tender point — which is what Simons found, in part; that a mental stressor raises activity at any endplate-zone site, not only the tender one; that the chemistry and the Doppler waveforms follow from compression of the bed by contracted fiber — which the imaging authors themselves list as a candidate cause; that felt releases occur without reproducible local transitions, or with equal transitions at sham sites and under pressure alone; that any fast mechanical change is densification thinning, with no perfusion change; that the sparks practitioners feel are hyperventilation paresthesias, tracking carbon dioxide and appearing at sham sites too; and that FDG uptake at knots is elevated, as contracting or inflamed tissue would show. *What the ledger holds.* This account needs no new physiology, and the only direct arteriole measurements available fit it better than they fit a latch. Its gap is the set of localized objective findings a purely central or interpretive story must still explain: a graded stiff region that blinded sonographers can measure, electrical activity that a mental task turns up at one point and not a centimeter away, abnormal local chemistry and flow. And it shares one weakness with its rivals — the observation base it explains was located by palpation, whose reliability is unproven. *What would decide it.* The same experiments, read the other way: a matched endplate-zone control site rising as much as the trigger point under arithmetic; stiffness dropping with no perfusion change; a hot knot on PET; sparks that track CO2 rather than the button press.

The three accounts agree on more than they dispute. All accept that people feel releases and that palpated points are measurably stiffer. All accept that slow breathing shifts autonomic state globally. All three, notably, say a knot is a state rather than a scar; the disagreement is about *which* state, in *which* tissue, held by *what*. And all three make predictions about the same seconds-long event nobody has filmed.

## The oldest anatomy text

{plate:IMG-VASO-P01}

Essentially every contemplative tradition that mapped the inner body arrived at the same three claims: there are knots, breath is the tool, and untying them changes consciousness. Tibetan tantric physiology describes channel-knots — rtsa mdud — constricting the flow of wind, untied by breath practice; Hindu yoga names the granthis; Chinese medicine records ashi points, tender spots named for the patient’s cry. The standard modern move is to file this as metaphor. The alternative reading is that [practitioners with extraordinarily trained interoception were producing first-person cartography of the vascular-autonomic tension system]{claim=VASO-C022} — channels as vasculature, winds as autonomic state, knots as latches or clenched bundles. The only record this ledger holds on the claim, in either direction, is the founding essay’s own uncited assertion that the traditional maps place the important knots along the torso’s midline and the limbs, where the sympathetic chains, dorsal root ganglia and dense fascia lie, rather than in the head. The perforator essay sharpens the proposal — classical points as perforators, the “knotting” places of the Chinese sinew channels as the bony lines where the fascial sheet is anchored — and that sharpening is useful precisely because it can be coded blind and tested against chance. Nobody has done so. Until someone does, every convergence is vulnerable to post-hoc matching — and even a genuine alignment with vascular geography would not show that anything latches or clenches. The traditions also preserved a warning, which this case records without adopting a mechanism: releasing held material faster than the system can integrate is destabilizing.

## The crux, and what would change our mind

Strip everything away and the disagreement is narrower than any camp admits. The dispute funnels into one empirical question: when a knot “releases” on a slow exhale, does anything objective happen locally — a stiffness drop, a perfusion rise, time-locked to the breath, exceeding what pressure alone, expectation, and generalized relaxation produce? Behind it sit two more. If something does happen, is the releasing element a vessel, and if so which one — an arteriole in the muscle or a perforator under the skin? And is the breath a key at all, or does pressure suffice?

What would move this case toward a vascular account:

- Time-resolved imaging of a felt release showing stiffness falling and perfusion rising together within seconds of the exhale, at palpated sites but not sham sites, with the vascular ordering — blood first, stiffness second.
- A local flash of skin perfusion time-locked to the exhale and the felt star, absent at sham sites and blocked when pressure is applied during an inhale-and-hold — the perforator signature.
- Blinded tender points coinciding with Doppler-mapped perforators above chance; a knot released by saline hydrodissection at its perforator with no breath.
- A pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after its stimulus is withdrawn, with falling phosphorylation and measured low energetic cost — the latch, in the vessel the original account needs.
- A palpated knot that is stiff on elastography and electrically active on EMG yet metabolically cold on FDG-PET.
- A retrieved primary study showing sympathetic blockade quiets the electrical nidus.
- A repeat of the mental-arithmetic experiment in which the trigger point rises and a matched endplate-zone control site does not — or a skin-perfusion fall over the point and not over control skin.
- In an animal, different induced vascular states producing reliably different later neural responses under identical stimulation, with oxygenation clamped.

What would move it toward the conventional account:

- Felt releases without reproducible local transitions, or equal transitions at sham sites and under pressure alone.
- Fascial densification reversing in seconds under pressure with no perfusion change — a fast, non-vascular state.
- Sparks whose perfusion correlates are global, equal at sham sites, and track carbon dioxide rather than the button press.
- Elevated FDG uptake at palpated knots.
- A matched endplate-zone control site rising as much as the trigger point under mental arithmetic.
- Tender points falling on perforators no more often than chance.
- A paired-caliber study finding the non-latching motor-protein phenotype throughout skeletal-muscle arterioles.
- A knot census with pain-free controls finding that Doppler measures do not pick out the palpated spots.

## Where the ledger stands

The verdict is *unresolved*, and that is a finding rather than a shrug. The ladder is inverted: the best-evidenced rungs — the latch exists, slow breathing shifts the autonomic system, vessels can nudge neurons, palpated points are stiffer — are the least *diagnostic*, meaning they are exactly what conventional physiology predicts too and so decide nothing between the accounts. The rungs that would decide the case — that a release is objective, that the releasing element is vascular, that the breath is necessary — are the ones with no evidence located, in either direction. The claim most exposed is the knot-as-latched-arteriole attribution, because the arteriole record leans against it and the vascular footprint at real trigger points is partial. The competing perforator account has, so far, nothing behind it but a proponent’s essay — it is featured here because it is a genuinely different mechanism with cheap tests, not because anything supports it. The observation most easily misread is the electrical nidus: real, stress-reactive, but more common at trigger points rather than exclusive to them, and living in the endplate zone. The claim the whole case hangs from is the felt release, which is credible as an experience and worthless, on its own, as a mechanism.

The strongest argument for the vascular hypothesis that this verdict does not answer is worth stating plainly. The classic energy-crisis account of trigger points has never explained how a fiber stays maximally contracted for years without exhausting itself; a latch would, and a clenched skin arteriole, which the body already pays to hold all day, would not need to. The electrical signature is millimeter-scale and stress-reactive while surrounding muscle stays quiet, which is odd for diffuse guarding even if the signature also appears at a minority of other endplate-zone sites. Attention has now been shown to regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site without arousal. Every arteriole study that found maintained activation kept its stimulus on, so none could have seen a state that persists after input stops — the very thing a knot would be. The skin bed is breath-gated in seconds by textbook reflex and site-addressable by ordinary blushing, so the perforator version asks for no new physiology either. And the hypothesis makes a timing prediction no rival makes — perfusion changes before stiffness — which is falsifiable and cheap. None of this is evidence that knots are vessels. It is a reason the experiments are worth running.

## The research agenda

The keystone experiment — ultrafast elastography and sensitive Doppler over a palpated knot, sites fixed in advance by blinded examiners, calibrated pressure through an instrumented probe, factorial controls, a button press at each felt release, and a mental-arithmetic block to catch stiffening during a purely cognitive event — would cost less than a mid-size grant and has never been run. It leads a program of nineteen items, ranked by how much each would decide. Second is its cheap surface cousin: a laser speckle camera over a knot on the occiput or upper trapezius, with exhale, inhale-hold, sham-site and carbon-dioxide controls, which discriminates the perforator, hyperventilation and no-local-event accounts at once. Then the paired-caliber arteriole study with a stimulus-withdrawal phase; the retrieval of six located-but-unopened papers, above all the runners’ elastography study that may hold the first objective imaged record of a fast release under pressure alone; the mental-arithmetic repeat with a matched endplate-zone control; the perforator coincidence map; the hydrodissection trial; the densification timescale; the FDG-PET overlay; the phentolamine search; the factorial trial separating the probe from the permission; the fibromyalgia-era community surveys as a proto-census; the census nobody has taken — there is no graph of knot burden against age, anywhere — with pain-free controls, children and long-term meditators; the animal experiment separating vascular memory from vascular plumbing; the blinded coding of the contemplative maps; the knot-free practitioner as a natural experiment, with a sensory exam to rule out a numbed finder; the retrieval of the primaries behind the euphoria and adverse-effect reports and behind the perforator essay’s citations; and the evidence map of the latch, already executed and reported above. A full-body ultrasound scanner announced in 2026 makes whole-body coverage imaginable, but it is a prototype built for body composition, not for the stiffness and flow channels a census needs, and it has no diagnostic clearance.

The machines exist. The practitioners exist. The experiments are small and specified. Someone should count. Either way, the knots are there. Press into one, and breathe out slowly.

assessment.synthesis: The ledger's ladder is inverted: the mechanism rung — latch physiology (VASO-E003), the slow-breathing autonomic shift (VASO-E009), vascular-to-neural mechanosensation in rat brain (VASO-E005) — is better evidenced than either the observations beneath it or the attributions above it, and every one of those records is credible without being diagnostic, because conventional physiology predicts each of them too. The observation base rests on two primaries. Ballyns 2011 gives the stiffness component of VASO-C005 blinded-sonographer support (VASO-E023: graded stiff area 0.57/0.36/0.17 cm², AUC 0.9) and a group-level Doppler difference (VASO-E022), but the same source shows the vascular signature is partial — retrograde flow at 31% of palpably normal sites, a null resistivity index, a pulsatility index that cannot classify sites, no pain-free controls, conduit-caliber vessels 1–2 cm from the point (VASO-E024, E025, E026) — and its authors list contracture compression as a co-equal cause of the flow pattern, so VASO-E027 is weighed as a qualifier at zero diagnosticity rather than as support, as its second reader argued. Simons 2002 (VASO-E031, E032) makes the electrical nidus a prevalence gradient that tracks the endplate zone first (11/11, 4/11, 0), lowering the diagnosticity of VASO-C002 and exposing the unmatched control site in VASO-C003. The anchor observation, a seconds-scale release on an exhale (VASO-C004), is supported only by proponent testimony (VASO-E014); the only imaged change in a trigger point is over visits after needling (VASO-E030); and the two-key necessity (VASO-C039) may be contradicted by a located-but-unretrieved 2025 elastography study reported to show release under pressure alone (VASO-R012). Where the original thesis needs the latch, the record points the other way: pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained or rising phosphorylation (VASO-E020), no arteriole energetic measurement exists (VASO-E019), and latch behaviour vanished one branch order downstream in the only paired comparison (VASO-E021). The essay-derived records VASO-E033–E043 are derivative restatements or hypothesis statements at zero independent weight; VASO-E039 is the sole record on VASO-C022 and leaves it untested. The records from the second proponent essay (VASO-E044, E045, E047, E050, E051, E052) rest on SRC-JHONG-2026A, which is unverified and by its own note may bear no weight; they are recorded here only to mark that a second vascular account — the stuck perforator (VASO-C174), which drops the latch and relocates the vessel to the superficial fascia — is now on the map with no evidence for or against it and cheap tests (VASO-R015, R016, R017) that would decide it. The memory attribution (VASO-C021) fails the write–store–read test (VASO-E017). Sensitivity: no single removal flips the case verdict, because neither direction holds decisive evidence. The record whose removal would most change the shape of the case is VASO-E020 — without it VASO-C020 reverts from 'examined in its named compartment and mismatched' to merely 'untested', and the perforator relocation loses its motivation. VASO-E016 remains the single most important undermining record; VASO-E031 most constrains the reading of the observations. Unresolved is a finding, not a default: three accounts of the same seconds-long event are specified, the decisive experiments are cheap and unrun, and every outcome remains live.
assessment.steelman: The classic energy-crisis account of trigger points has never explained how a skeletal-muscle fiber could remain near-maximally contracted for years without exhausting itself; a latch is the one known physiological device that holds tension for almost nothing, and a clenched skin arteriole, which the body demonstrably pays to hold all day, would not even need the economy — so the puzzle the conventional account cannot dissolve is exactly the one both vascular accounts dissolve. The electrical signature is confined to one to two millimeters and is selectively turned up by mental arithmetic while surrounding muscle stays quiet; that it also appears at four of eleven other endplate-zone sites does not explain why it is present at eleven of eleven trigger points, nor why a stressor picks the tender one. Blinded sonographers find a graded stiff region at exactly the sites examiners palpate, and the arteries nearby behave differently — the footprint a throttled bed would leave, whatever else could leave it. Voluntary attention has now been shown, in preregistered human experiments, to regulate a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site with no change in arousal — the write channel the synthesis needs, demonstrated. Every arteriole study reporting maintained activation held its stimulus present throughout, so none could have detected a state that persists after input stops, which is the only state a knot requires; and the latch-competent versus latch-incompetent phenotype has never been surveyed in skeletal-muscle arterioles under chronic sympathetic drive. The perforator version asks for no new physiology at all: the skin bed is constricted by a deep breath within two seconds by a textbook reflex, opened by a slow exhale, addressed site by site every time a person blushes, and history-dependent after cold — and medicine already recognizes a class of exquisitely tender points where a vessel-nerve bundle pierces a fascial ring, relieved by freeing the ring. Finally, the vascular hypothesis makes distinctive, falsifiable predictions that neither guarding nor densification makes — perfusion rises before stiffness falls; a knot released by hydrodissection without breath; a stiff, active spot that is metabolically cold — and all of them can be tested for the cost of a small grant, one of them with a pencil Doppler in an afternoon. None of this shows that knots are vessels; it is the best reason the assessment cannot yet be closed against them.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: Muscle knots are maintained vascular-autonomic states rather than structural lesions. In the original form of the claim, the state is microvascular smooth muscle inside the muscle held in the latch-bridge state, throttling local blood flow and sensitizing local nerve endings, with secondary skeletal-muscle guarding layered on top. In a second form from the same proponent, the state is a cutaneous perforator — a small artery, nerve and lymphatic passing together through a ring in the superficial fascia — held constricted by ordinary sympathetic tone, collared by gelled hyaluronan and tethering the fascial sheet, needing no latch at all. In either form the knot is writable by stress, readable as stiffness and ache, and releasable by sustained pressure combined with slow exhalation. More broadly, vascular tension functions as a memory element participating in mental life, the physical implementation of what contemplative traditions call clinging, and the traditional anatomies of knots and channels are first-person maps of the same system.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether people feel tender spots, not over whether palpated points are measurably stiffer, not over whether smooth muscle can latch, and not even over state versus scar — all three live accounts say a knot is a state. The crux is whether anything objective happens locally when a knot 'releases' on a slow exhale: does stiffness fall and perfusion rise within seconds, time-locked to the breath, beyond what pressure alone, expectation and generalized relaxation produce? Behind it sit three further disputes. Which tissue holds the state: an arteriole inside the muscle (where the published record shows maintained activation, not a latch), a perforator under the skin (where nothing has been measured at all), a stress-sensitive skeletal endplate under central guarding, or gelled fascial hyaluronan? Is the breath necessary — or does pressure suffice, as a located-but-unretrieved elastography study is reported to show? And does the brain address the knot or merely the endplate zone, given that the electrical signature also appears at a minority of non-tender endplate-zone sites? Beneath all of it, the skeptical literature disputes whether the trigger point is reliably identifiable at all.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A time-locked imaging experiment: ultrafast shear-wave elastography and sensitive microvascular Doppler over a palpated knot during breath-assisted release, with sites fixed in advance by blinded examiners, calibrated pressure through an instrumented probe, factorial controls (pressure with normal breathing, slow breathing without pressure, pressure during an inhale-and-hold, sham sites, failed attempts), a button press at each felt release, and a preregistered prediction that stiffness drops and perfusion rises together within seconds of the exhale, exceeding all controls, with perfusion leading stiffness. Felt releases without reproducible local transitions, or equal transitions at shams and under pressure alone, would return the knot to the guarding-and-interpretation account. A surface variant with laser speckle contrast imaging and end-tidal CO2 discriminates the perforator, hyperventilation and no-local-event readings at once. Companion studies decide the compartment and the localization: a blinded pencil-Doppler coincidence map of tender points against perforators; ultrasound-guided saline hydrodissection at a mapped perforator with no breath; a paired-caliber, pressurized arteriole preparation with a stimulus-withdrawal phase; a repeat of the mental-arithmetic experiment with a matched endplate-zone control site; a small FDG-PET overlay testing whether stiff, active knots are metabolically cold; a retrieved densification timescale; and a Doppler census with pain-free controls, since every existing flow comparison sits inside symptomatic muscle.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Tenderness and its relief need no vascular memory. Tender points are neuromuscular guarding — sustained low-level motor drive and endplate activity in skeletal muscle, centrally maintained and stress-sensitive — possibly with altered fascial gliding from hyaluronan densification between fascial layers. The electrical signature is endplate noise, a property of the endplate zone that is more prevalent where tissue is tender; a stressor that raises sympathetic drive to endplates would raise it. The acidic, mediator-rich milieu follows from compression under guarding as readily as from a throttled vessel, and the high-resistance Doppler waveforms near trigger points are, by the imaging authors' own account, as compatible with contracture squeezing the capillary bed as with distal constriction — while a second resistance index shows no difference at all. The felt release is expectation and attention doing what they demonstrably do, riding the genuine but global parasympathetic shift of slow breathing, with pressure altering local sensation; any rapid mechanical change is densification thinning or guarding switching off, not a vessel unlatching or a perforator reopening; the sparks practitioners feel are hyperventilation paresthesias, global and CO2-tracking rather than local. Nothing is stored locally: the brain stops guarding, regionally or globally, and interpretation supplies the rest. A stricter version adds that manual trigger-point identification has poor examiner reliability and no validated reference standard, so part of the observation base may be an artifact of training and expectation. This account requires no new physiology, and the only direct arteriole measurements available fit it better than they fit a latch. Its gap is the set of localized objective findings — a graded stiff region that blinded sonographers can measure, spontaneous electrical activity that a mental task selectively raises at one point, abnormal local chemistry and flow — that a purely central or interpretive story must still account for.

components.label: The observation base: tender points, their measurable correlates, and the felt release
components.note: Palpated points are objectively stiffer in a graded way under blinded imaging and chemically abnormal; the flow signature is partial and confined to symptomatic muscle; the seconds-scale felt release and the necessity of breath rest on proponent testimony; and the reliability of the palpable spot itself is disputed in the peer-reviewed literature.

components.label: The neural signature: an addressable, stress-reactive nidus
components.note: Real and turned up by mental arithmetic, but a prevalence gradient that tracks the endplate zone first (11/11, 4/11, 0); the control site was never matched to the endplate zone; three readings — stress-sensitive endplates, an intramuscular vascular write, a regional skin vasoconstriction — fit the same needle.

components.label: The latch, and its reach into the vessels a knot would need
components.note: Textbook in conduit arteries; in pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles maintained constriction tracks maintained or rising phosphorylation, no arteriole's energetic cost has ever been measured, and latch behaviour vanished one branch order downstream in the only paired comparison.

components.label: The autonomic lever: breath and attention
components.note: Slow breathing reproducibly shifts autonomic balance globally; voluntary attention regulates a peripheral vascular bed at a chosen site over tens of minutes by a vagal immune route. The local, seconds-scale unlatching or reopening at a tender point that every vascular account adds has never been measured.

components.label: The read path: vessels modulate neurons
components.note: Demonstrated as instantaneous mechanosensitive modulation in rat brain; storage, peripheral operation and content-specific readout remain undemonstrated.

components.label: The attributions: latched arteriole, stuck perforator, vascular memory, contemplative maps
components.note: No direct evidence for any. The latched-arteriole form is mismatched with the arteriole record; the perforator form rests on an unverified proponent essay and has never been tested; the memory identification fails the write–store–read criteria; the maps have never been coded blind against chance.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive experiments are small, specified and unrun; both directions are live for every one of them; a laser-speckle surface variant and a pencil-Doppler coincidence map cost almost nothing and discriminate three accounts at once; a single located-but-unretrieved paper may already hold the first objective imaged fast release; and the phenomenon is available in millions of bodies.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Records: VASO-E013 (Johnson's three hypotheses, context), VASO-E038 (essay relay, context), VASO-E017 (critical report: hysteresis is not memory; the write–store–read sequence has never been shown; the nearest demonstrated flow-network memory is Physarum). No record supports the identification directly and none contradicts it. Its dependency rungs (VASO-C010, VASO-C012) are credible but describe force maintenance and instantaneous modulation, not storage with content-specific readout.

treatment.plainLanguage: The tension in blood-vessel walls is claimed to be a physical form of memory — the body's implementation of holding on to an expectation.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The case's outermost thesis; nothing in the ledger bears on it, so at present it discriminates nothing.
treatment.strongestObjection: A thermostat has hysteresis without an autobiography: no experiment shows a vascular state that depends on prior input, is read out later, and discriminates between different prior inputs; the only demonstrated flow-network memory is in a slime mold whose tubes are its own body.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R005: different induced vascular states biasing later neural responses under identical stimulation, with oxygenation clamped
Any demonstration that erasing a local vascular state selectively relaxes or erases a neural representation
A clean negative in VASO-R005 — gain effects only through instantaneous perfusion — would collapse this to ordinary neurovascular physiology

claimAssessments.reasoning: Undermined by VASO-E016 (grade D on both linchpins), VASO-E019 (no arteriole energetic measurement exists) and VASO-E020 (pressurized skeletal-muscle arterioles show maintained or rising phosphorylation). VASO-E027 is nominally supporting, but the source lists contracture compression as a co-equal cause and never mentions latch, so it is weighed as a qualifier at zero diagnosticity, as its second reader argued. VASO-E037 is the hypothesis statement. VASO-E044/E045, from an unverified source weighed at nothing, record only that the proponent's later essay accepts the arteriole audit and relocates the vessel, so the latched-arteriole form is now one of two vascular candidates. The three arteriole studies held their stimulus on throughout, so the absence of a latch signature there is a mismatch, not a refutation.

treatment.plainLanguage: A knot is a small blood vessel inside the muscle held shut by a molecular ratchet, starving its own neighbourhood.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis: its truth value decides the case, and its distinctive predictions — a metabolically cold spot, blood before stiffness, a latch-competent arteriole — separate it from guarding and from the perforator account.
treatment.strongestObjection: Where the compartment it names has been measured, maintained constriction tracks maintained activation, the opposite of the economical dephosphorylated hold a latch requires; no study identifies smooth-muscle latch at any tender point; and the vessels with abnormal Doppler are conduit-scale, a centimetre or two away.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R004: a pressurized skeletal-muscle arteriole holding constriction after stimulus withdrawal at falling phosphorylation and measured low energetic cost
VASO-R013: a stiff, electrically active knot that is cold on FDG-PET
VASO-R001: perfusion rising before stiffness falls at palpated sites, beyond all controls
Against: a hot knot on PET, or the non-latching motor-protein phenotype found throughout skeletal-muscle arterioles

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchored only to SRC-JHONG-2026A, an unverified, AI-generated proponent essay that may bear no weight; no evidence record supports or contradicts it. Featured because it is a genuinely different mechanism for the same phenomenon: it accepts the arteriole audit (VASO-E045), drops the latch, and relocates the vessel to the superficial perforator bed, with cheap discriminating tests (VASO-R015, R016, R017). Its parent identity proposition — that knots are stuck perforators — has no ledger record beyond the essay. It owes an account of the intramuscular stiff regions (VASO-E023) and hypoechoic nodules (VASO-E050).

treatment.plainLanguage: A knot is a small artery-and-nerve bundle where it pierces the fascia under the skin, held clenched by three things at once — the vessel's tone, a gel collar around it, and the tether it makes to the fascial sheet — none of which needs a latch.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If tender points coincide with Doppler-mapped perforators above chance and release by hydrodissection without breath, the knot acquires an anatomical identity no other test supplies; a null on the coincidence map removes this account in an afternoon.
treatment.strongestObjection: The instrumented stiff regions and hypoechoic nodules sit inside the trapezius muscle, not in the subcutaneous fascia; the supporting literature is restated second-hand from an unverified essay; and the ledger has no evidence that ordinary tender points sit on perforators.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R015: blinded tender points coinciding with pencil-Doppler perforators above chance
VASO-R017: release by saline hydrodissection at a mapped perforator with no breath or pressure
VASO-R016: a local skin-perfusion flash on exhale, absent at sham and blocked under inhale-hold
Against: coincidence at chance, or no effect of hydrodissection

claimAssessments.reasoning: Only VASO-E039 (weak, uncited proponent assertion about where the maps place knots), with no coding rule and no chance baseline. The perforator essay's sharper alignment — classical points as perforators, sinew-channel knots as fascial anchor lines, catalogued as VASO-C123 and C159–C161 — is unverified and unanchored to primaries, and the same essay names a multicentre dissection that found vessel–nerve bundles at only a few points.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ancient Tibetan, Indian and Chinese body maps are claimed to be accurate first-person charts of the same tension system.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even a real alignment with vascular geography would show the maps are anatomical, not that the mechanism is vascular or that anything latches or clenches.
treatment.strongestObjection: Post-hoc matching: locations are being read after the modern candidates are known, and no blinded coding against chance has ever been done.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R006: preregistered blinded coding of rtsa mdud, granthi and ashi locations aligning with vascular, autonomic or fascial geography above chance
VASO-R019: retrieval of Heine 1988, Langevin & Yandow 2002, Dorsher 2009 and Maurer 2019 to test the perforator version of the alignment
Coding at chance would retire the convergence argument

claimAssessments.reasoning: VASO-E003 strong (Hai & Murphy kinetic model of dephosphorylated attached cross-bridges); VASO-E034 is a weak restatement that overstates the model. VASO-E021 qualifies: latch present in rabbit femoral artery and absent one branch order downstream in its saphenous branch (42% vs 28% phosphorylation, 40% stress loss), never followed further. The capability is textbook; its generality across vessel types is not.

treatment.plainLanguage: Blood-vessel muscle can lock in place and hold tension cheaply after the signal that triggered it fades.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Common ground for every account; nobody disputes the latch exists in conduit arteries, so it decides nothing about knots.
treatment.strongestObjection: Demonstrated in large tonic arteries with maintained low-level activation; not shown in any arteriole, and lost one branch order downstream in the only paired comparison.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R004 paired-caliber study finding latch capacity extending into skeletal-muscle arterioles
Or finding the non-latching phenotype throughout — which would leave the claim true but irrelevant to knots

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on physiological priors — remodeling takes days to weeks — rather than any record; VASO-E035 is the argument itself, and VASO-E030 shows imaged measures moving over visits after needling, not seconds. Its premise, an objective seconds-scale local event, is unmeasured (VASO-E016). State is a broader category than vascular: guarding and densification (VASO-C077) are also states.

treatment.plainLanguage: If a knot really lets go in seconds, whatever let go was something the body was actively doing, not scar tissue.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides scar against state, which all three live accounts already accept; it does not decide vessel against guarding against densification.
treatment.strongestObjection: The conditional's antecedent has never been observed; the only fast-release report is proponent testimony.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R012: Olewnik 2025 retrieved and showing palpated foci undetectable on elastography within minutes of pressure and absent at 24 hours
VASO-R001: a time-locked local transition
Felt releases with no objective local transition would remove the premise

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; the primary Stecco literature has not been retrieved. Featured as the conventional account's candidate for a fast, non-vascular state. The critical report characterizes densification as a plausible mechanism for altered fascial sliding but not an established explanation for trigger points, and notes that hyaluronan does not show a simple age effect.

treatment.plainLanguage: The lubricant between fascial layers can thicken like a gel and thin again with pressure, movement and warmth — a stiff spot that is neither scar nor vessel.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If densification reverses in seconds, a stiffness drop without a perfusion rise becomes a live reading of any imaged release; if it takes minutes to hours, the vascular accounts remain the only candidates for a seconds-scale objective event.
treatment.strongestObjection: No study reports the reversal timescale under load; the evidence is anatomical and cadaveric; and densification alone does not explain why a mental stressor turns up electrical activity at the spot.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R008: a retrieved measured or modelled timescale of hyaluronan viscosity change under pressure and warmth
VASO-R001: stiffness dropping with flat perfusion at a release
VASO-R017: hydrodissection releasing a knot, which both the collar and perforator readings predict

claimAssessments.reasoning: VASO-E004 is the hypothesis paper (context); VASO-E005 is strong — blood-pressure pulsations modulate neurons via mechanosensitive channels in rat brain on rapid timescales. Instantaneous modulation is shown; storage, peripheral operation and content-specificity are not.

treatment.plainLanguage: Blood vessels can nudge nearby nerve cells, not just feed them.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A read path is necessary for the memory thesis but is equally consistent with a world in which nothing is stored; it decides nothing about knots.
treatment.strongestObjection: Rat cortex, instantaneous mechanosensation; nonspecific ischemic suppression of firing would look the same without any information content.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A peripheral demonstration at sensory endings adjacent to the vessels whose caliber they would sense
VASO-R005: history-dependent readout beyond instantaneous perfusion, with oxygenation clamped

claimAssessments.reasoning: VASO-E009 is a strong systematic review of slow-breathing studies in healthy humans (heart-rate variability, respiratory sinus arrhythmia); VASO-E036 is a weak uncited restatement. Global cardiovascular indices only; no local tissue or tender-point measurement.

treatment.plainLanguage: Breathing slowly, especially exhaling slowly, reliably tilts the nervous system toward its rest-and-digest mode.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Accepted by all accounts; the local, site-specific unlatching or reopening the vascular accounts add has never been measured.

whatWouldChangeOurMind: VASO-R003: a factorial trial showing breath adds nothing local beyond relaxation
VASO-R001: local effects at the knot exceeding the global shift

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record; anchored only to the unverified second essay. It is the perforator account's reading of VASO-E002 and competes with the guarding and intramuscular readings. Site-specific sympathetic control of skin flow is ordinary physiology, but nothing has measured skin perfusion over a tender point during a stressor.

treatment.plainLanguage: The knot lighting up during a math test is the brain clenching the skin's blood vessels over that spot, the way it makes you blush.

treatment.strongestObjection: The signal McNulty recorded is skeletal-muscle electrophysiology a centimetre or more deep; a skin-vessel event has to explain a needle reading in muscle.

treatment.plainLanguage: Pushing on a knot without the breath is said not to release it.

treatment.strongestObjection: The trigger-point treatment literature — ischemic compression, dry needling — reports releasing points routinely without breath instruction, and the one imaged fast release on record is reported under pressure alone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: No evidence record. A prediction shared by both vascular accounts (latch and perforator) and made by neither guarding nor densification. The ordering of vessel, stiffness and nerve changes at a release has never been measured in any tissue.

treatment.plainLanguage: If a knot is a clenched vessel, blood should come back a moment before the tissue softens.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The single most discriminating measurable in the case: perfusion leading stiffness favours a vascular state; stiffness leading or moving alone favours guarding or densification.
treatment.strongestObjection: Decompression of a bed squeezed by guarding could reperfuse essentially simultaneously with softening, so the ordering needs frame rates fast enough to resolve it — and it does not separate latch from perforator.
